items.text: SEASON 6 · EPISODE 7 · DRAFT  Design studio and courthouse · Maya, Anselm, Odile and Judge Obi · Level L4 · Intermediate support  In the mock-up of Courtroom 1, two jurors say the witness sounds far away. Everyone else is fine.  ⚑ RV-141: figures illustrative. The ceiling is the architect’s; ducts the mechanical engineer’s. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Coverage
items.stakes: Two jurors in the mock-up say the witness sounds far away. Everyone else is fine. The sign-off is Thursday.
items.reward: Every seat covered — the jury's first.

objectives.text: Look closer: two things about Courtroom 1

items.rumor: The room averaged fine. The worst seats in it belonged to the jury.

items.alt: The full-size mock-up of Courtroom 1: Judge Obi by the jury box; Maya listening from the witness box.

bubbles.text: Two of my mock jurors say the witness sounds far away.
Only two? Then it's where they're sitting.

items.caption: Sign-off is Thursday.

lines.text: Two of my mock jurors say the witness sounds far away. In a real trial, ‘far away’ is a verdict on the wrong evidence.
Then we find out exactly where it's far away.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #58 · AVERY'S LENS  Check the seat that matters most  An average across a room hides the one seat where it fails — look for the worst position, and make sure it isn't the one that counts.  Courtroom 1 averaged fine. The worst seats in the room were the jury's.

items.alt: Drawing AV-220: ceiling loudspeakers on a 6 m square grid, each with a green coverage circle 6 m across that just touches its neighbours, leaving white gaps between every four; the jury box in a corner under a dashed bulkhead.
items.caption: Circles that touch — and gaps where four of them meet.

items.prompt: I drew that grid. Six metres, edge to edge, the way I've always done it.

options.label: “Edge-to-edge leaves the middle of every four uncovered. Can we try 4.2 and survey it?”
options.reply: Thirty years and nobody made me stand in the middle. Go on.

items.prompt: Noon. Two jurors hear less. How do you find out why?
items.risk: A jury that hears the witness less than the public does.
timeout: The afternoon goes on arguing about the microphone.

hints.text: Where is it worst — and what's different there?

options.label: Turn the system up 6 dB
options.result: The gallery complains it's too loud; the jury box is still 6 dB behind.
options.fail: More level everywhere doesn't fix one seat.

options.label: Survey level at seated ear height across the room, then check the geometry
options.result: −6 dB in the jury box and at every point between four loudspeakers.
options.consequence: Find the worst seats, then why.

options.label: Swap the witness microphone
options.result: The new mic sounds the same in the jury box.
options.consequence: The witness is fine in the gallery.

options.label: Move the two jurors
options.result: In a real trial, jurors sit where the court puts them.
options.consequence: The seats belong to the court.

items.title: Edge to edge.
items.body: At 4.2 m ceiling and 1.2 m seated ears, a 90° loudspeaker covers a circle 6.0 m across — and the grid is 6.0 m. Edge to edge. But the point between four loudspeakers is 6.0 ÷ √2 = 4.24 m from each, and coverage reaches only 3.0 m. Every square of the grid has a hole in the middle.
items.label: Test: how far is the worst point — and what spacing closes it?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Anselm and Maya beside a board. Coverage at ear height: two times ceiling minus ear height, times the tangent of half the coverage angle. Four-point-two ceiling, one-point-two ears, ninety degrees… six metres across. The drawing spaces them six apart. Edge to edge. Now stand between four of them — you're four point two metres from each, and the cone only reaches three.

bubbles.text: Coverage at ear height: two times ceiling minus ear height, times the tangent of half the coverage angle.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Coverage angle   Ceiling loudspeaker   Ear height   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Ceiling loudspeaker spacing  D = 2 × (H c  − H e ) × tan(θ ÷ 2)   D  spacing for edge-to-edge coverage at ear height, m  H c   ceiling height, m  H e   ear height — about 1.2 m seated  θ  the loudspeaker's coverage angle, degrees

items.label: **Work it out:** space Courtroom 1's ceiling loudspeakers.
**Pick the clues:** why can't the jurors hear?

items.title: The bulkhead.
items.body: The reflected ceiling plan shows what the floor plan couldn't: over the jury box the ceiling drops to a 2.7 m bulkhead carrying a supply duct. Under it, a 90° loudspeaker covers only 3.0 m — and the jury box sits in the gap between two rings of the main grid.
items.label: Test: what's the coverage there — and who must agree a loudspeaker in the bulkhead?

items.prompt: Wednesday. How do you cover the jury box?
items.happening: Jury box in a gap under a bulkhead.
known: ◉ D = 6.0 m main · 3.0 m under the bulkhead
unknown: Where a loudspeaker can go in the bulkhead
items.risk: A jury that hears less than the gallery.
timeout: Thursday's sign-off happens with the jury box as it is.
The courthouse is built with the gap.

hints.text: Who owns the bulkhead — and what's inside it?

options.label: A 4.2 m grid, plus one loudspeaker in the bulkhead — positioned with Odile and the mechanical engineer clear of the duct and diffusers — and a re-survey
options.result: A spot between two diffusers, 300 mm off the duct. The re-survey: ±2 dB everywhere, jury box included.

options.label: Cut a loudspeaker into the bulkhead on the drawings
options.result: Odile: “That bulkhead holds a supply duct. Ask before you put a hole in it.”
options.consequence: Someone else's ceiling, someone else's duct.
options.fail: Never cut into another trade's work without asking.

options.label: Aim a wall loudspeaker at the jury box from the side
options.result: Now the jury hears the witness from the wall — and every word twice.

options.label: Tighten the grid to 3 m everywhere
options.result: Thirty loudspeakers; the jury box is still under the bulkhead.

items.title: Fifty thousand people and one voice
items.body: In September 1919, President Woodrow Wilson spoke to a crowd of about 50,000 in San Diego's stadium through an early electric public-address system — among the first times a crowd that size heard a speaker through loudspeakers. The engineers placed horns to cover the crowd, and the parts of the stands between them heard less. Coverage has been geometry ever since.

items.alt: The revised drawing: loudspeakers on a 4.2 m grid with overlapping green circles and no gaps, and one indigo loudspeaker in the bulkhead over the jury box.
items.caption: No holes — and one loudspeaker where the ceiling drops.

items.title: Bulkhead · 2.7 m
items.body: The reflected ceiling plan — the ceiling drawn as if seen in a mirror on the floor — shows a 2.7 m bulkhead over the jury box carrying a supply duct. The loudspeaker drawing was made on the floor plan, where ceilings have no height.

items.prompt: Thursday. How does coverage get checked on every project?
known: ◉ Floor plan had no ceiling heights

options.label: Draw coverage on the reflected ceiling plan at seated ear height, check the worst point on the grid, and survey the mock-up — jury and witness boxes first
options.result: Kit adds a ‘worst point’ check to the layout template.
options.consequence: Heights from the ceiling plan, the worst seat checked, and a measurement.

options.label: Always use a 3 m grid
options.result: Some rooms get twice the loudspeakers they need; others still have bulkheads.
options.consequence: A rule of thumb isn't a check.

options.label: Trust the maker's layout software
options.result: The software used the floor plan — no bulkhead.

options.label: Nothing — Courtroom 1 is fixed
options.result: Courtroom 2 has the same 6 m grid.

items.body: The survey sheet's worst reading: juror 4's chair, 6.2 dB below the room average. The best seat in the room is the public gallery's back row.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  D = 2 × (H_c − H_e) × tan(θ ÷ 2). On a square grid, spacing ≤ D ÷ √2 leaves no holes. Take ceiling heights from the reflected ceiling plan, find the worst seat — the jury’s and the witness’s first — and survey the mock-up. Ceilings are the architect’s; ducts are the mechanical engineer’s.
REFLECTION (optional)  · The room averaged fine. Where does an average hide a person in your work?
